query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Grain boundary sliding is the dominant deformation mechanism in high-entropy-alloy multilayers under sustained loading at elevated temperatures, due to the interaction between dislocation movement and multi-principal elemental atoms.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoscale multilayer coating with ultrafine-grained microstructure
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (500-600 °C) and constant applied stress
generation.mechanism: Dislocation movement and grain boundary sliding
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved creep resistance and deformation tolerance
generation.baseline: Conventional metallic multilayers with dislocation-dominated deformation
generation.boundary: Temperature and strain rate dependence of deformation mechanism
generation.uncertainty: Limited understanding of the role of short-range order and compositional complexity on deformation behavior

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile creep tests under constant stress on multiple fine-grained CoCrFeNiMn HEA specimens
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the creep resistance is not improved at elevated temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified

Hence, the introduction of elemental grain boundary segregation structures into ultrafine-grained RHEAs could be an excellent strategy to improve performance characteristics and enrich the microstructure control range.
Severe plastic deformation (SPD) is an effective approach to induce component element grain boundary segregation []. Both dislocations and defects generated during the deformation supply a driving force for the segregation behavior of solute atoms. The SPD techniques, such as surface mechanical grinding treatment and high-pressure torsion, have been successfully applied for Al and Mg alloys to obtain the grain boundary segregation structure and corresponding expected properties [,]. Notably, these methods are based on a considerable plasticity and acceptable deformation resistance at room temperature. However, for the ultrafine-grained RHEAs, the exceedingly high strength and limited ductility have brought considerable challenges to the SPD process. This intrinsic mechanism indicated effective heat-resistance during high-temperature plastic deformation processes. Owing to the aforementioned sluggish elemental diffusion, it is optimistic that the CoCrFeNiMn alloy will exhibit a promising perspective in high-temperature applications.
When referring to high-temperature performance for most alloy systems, creep resistance is one of the most important standards for service life and safety reliability of engineering structures.
